science.title: Positional isomerisation of pyridine via nitrogen transposition
science.description: Positional isomers of pyridines often display distinct biological activities1,2 yet their direct interconversion remains largely inaccessible, so each isomer is typically prepared through an independent synthesis. Here we report a general strategy for pyridine positional isomerization enabled by controlled reorganization of the heteroaromatic core through sequential nitrogen insertion and deletion. N-atom transposition allows predictable translocation of preinstalled substituents without altering substituent identity. The method is broadly applicable to mono-, di-, and multisubstituted pyridines and operates across structurally complex molecular environments, providing direct access to positional isomers. This work establishes positional isomerization as a practical synthetic transformation, defining pyridine substitution patterns as mutable variables in retrosynthetic design.

science.title: In Argentina, one fossil bone from a 236-million-year-old cynodont contained a rare clue about birth. Researchers found its newborn size resembled mammals, suggesting live birth evolved 95 million yea
science.description: New fossil evidence challenges the long-held belief that ancient cynodonts laid eggs. A recent study found compelling proof that Chiniquodon theotonicus gave birth to live young. This discovery pushes the evolutionary timeline for live birth back by approximately ninety-five million years. Such an adaptation offered better protection for developing embryos in harsh Triassic environments. This finding suggests some early mammalian ancestors were more like modern mammals than previously assumed.

science.title: Aggregation-induced ultra-narrowband emission with a spectral FWHM of 13 nm
science.description: The inherent aggregation-induced spectral broadening of organic narrowband emitters limits their practical applications. To address this challenge, Chinese researchers proposed a molecular conformation control strategy based on a central 8π-electron system, and successfully realized a groundbreaking photophysical phenomenon: Aggregation-induced ultra-narrowband emission (AIUNE). This unique AIUNE character demonstrates superiority in highly-doped OLED devices, achieving a record-narrowed electroluminescent FWHM of 13 nm. This research expands the library of narrowband emission materials and enriches relevant molecular design methodologies.

science.title: Boosting the elimination of bacteria via a metal-free LED/visible-light photocatalytic-antibiotic strategy
science.description: Microbial pollutants continue to threaten aquatic environments and human health, creating an increasing demand for efficient, sustainable, and innovative antibacterial technologies. Metal-free photocatalysts offer a safer and more sustainable route for water disinfection; however, their potential interactions with antibiotics remain insufficiently understood. Here, graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) photocatalysts were synthesized via melamine polymerization under controlled CO2-atmospheres to tailor their surface and optical properties. Four variants (CN-Air, CN-LF, CN-MF, and CN-HF) were obtained and systematically characterized. CN-LF, produced under low CO2 flow, exhibited the highest surface area, enhanced visible-light absorption, and superior photocatalytic performance. Its antibacterial interaction with eight widely used antibiotics (gentamicin, amoxicillin, ampicillin, amoxiclav, azithromycin, cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, and tetracycline) was quantified using checkerboard assays (FICI) and inhibition-zone enhancement tests. CN-LF exhibited borderline synergistic interactions with ampicillin and cefuroxime (FICI = 0.5, at the synergy threshold), corresponding to 40% and 200% increases in antibacterial activity, respectively. Overall, these findings demonstrate that CO2-engineered g-C3N4 provides a sustainable, metal-free platform to enhance antibiotic performance via a light-associated cooperative mechanism, suggesting a potential strategy for improving antibacterial performance and contributing to environmental safety.

science.title: Unlocking Gondwana’s 120-million-year archive: Comprehensive synthesis explains palaeo-climate dynamics, extinction events, and evolution in South Africa’s Karoo Basin
science.description:
A comprehensive synthesis published in the South African Journal of Geology evaluates 25 years of research on the Karoo Supergroup, an exceptional ~120-million-year rock record spanning the Late Carboniferous to Early Jurassic. Integrating multi-proxy sedimentology, U-Pb geochronology, magnetostratigraphy, and palaeontology, the review evaluates long-standing basin models and refines the stratigraphic architecture across southern Gondwana.
The synthesised data challenge simplistic models of linear aridification, revealing non-linear palaeoclimate oscillations – including short-lived pluvial episodes in the Carnian (Late Triassic) and extensive lacustrine-erg interactions in the Pliensbachian (Early Jurassic). Furthermore, it spotlights the improved resolution of the Karoo biozonation, a core of studies on palaeo-ecosystem dynamics, and documents patterns of ecological collapse, persistence, and recovery across four major deep-time biocrises: the end-Capitanian, end-Permian, end-Triassic, and end-Pliensbachian. This synthesis establishes an updated framework to resolve intra-basin heterogeneity and optimise the correlation of Pan-Gondwanan tectonic-climatic events.

science.title: New 3D-printable cellulose hydrogel defies freezing temperatures for wearable sensors
science.description: Researchers have developed a cellulose-based hydrogel sensor that maintains stable sensing performance in extreme cold using a zinc chloride and lithium bromide molten salt hydrate system, offering a sustainable and biodegradable platform for next-generation flexible wearable devices and human-machine interfaces. Published in Journal of Bioresources and Bioproducts, the study introduces a binary molten salt hydrate approach to dissolve natural cellulose efficiently within ten minutes. The resulting ionically conductive hydrogel achieves an impressive conductivity of 4.48 S/m and compressive strength of 2.48 MPa. Differential scanning calorimetry confirmed no water crystallization exothermic peaks from -80°C to 20°C, indicating exceptional anti-freezing capability. The material's shear-thinning properties further enable 3D printing of customized sensor geometries for human-machine interfaces.
